def: A system property where identical inputs can produce different responses; agents are this kind of system, breaking the traditional 'reproduce and set a breakpoint' debugging intuition.
pitfall: Thinking you can run it a few more times and eventually hit the same path—you'll hit a different but equally valid path instead, burning tokens.
distractor_rationale: Often conflated with intermittent concurrency bugs—but those at least run on the same deterministic code; agents make decisions at every step.

def: When one step fails and causes the agent to explore an entirely different trajectory, with all subsequent turns growing on the wrong branch, leading to unpredictable outcomes.
pitfall: Only looking at the terminal output for problems—the actual lesion is often dozens of turns back at a timeout or error.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as 'model hallucination' when the starting point is usually a small glitch that would only be worth one retry log entry in a traditional service.

def: Agents are stateful and errors compound; agents can run for long periods maintaining state across many tool calls, so errors accumulate turn by turn.
pitfall: Restarting from the beginning when errors occur—expensive and frustrating for users, and if state at failure time wasn't recorded, there's no way to resume.
distractor_rationale: Easily confused with 'context grows longer': that's just a cost problem, compounding is the error itself amplifying.

def: Behaviors in multi-agent systems that arise without specific programming—for instance, small changes to the lead agent unpredictably changing subagent behavior.
pitfall: Only testing individual agent behavior and thinking you've covered it—what you really need to understand is interaction patterns.
distractor_rationale: Sounds mystical, but refers to specific observable phenomena—spawning 50 subagents for simple queries, distracting each other with excessive updates.

def: The terminal-state scoring, validators, and evaluation sets built in the previous course—answers only 'did it break,' not 'why.'
pitfall: Using a single fail line as diagnostic conclusion; the scorer stands at the finish line holding up a scorecard, it has no ability to care about the middle segment.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as a substitute for observability when they're actually two ends of one pole: evaluation judges good or bad, observation investigates cause.

def: Building simulations using the exact same prompts and tools from your system, then watching agents work step-by-step.
pitfall: Smoothing out prompts 'to make it clearer' so you can observe better—then you're observing a different system.
distractor_rationale: Often misread as 'reproduce the same run' when the real point is 'see each step.'

def: The middle layers frameworks add to simplify calling LLMs, defining tools, and chaining calls—they obscure underlying prompts and responses.
pitfall: Incorrect assumptions about what's under the hood are a common source of customer error; using frameworks requires understanding the underlying code.
distractor_rationale: Looks similar to 'no records' but the causes are opposite: one is obscured, one was never retained—both hurt equally when you need evidence after the fact.

def: An isolated environment where agents that can take action undergo extensive testing, used with appropriate guardrails.
pitfall: Thinking 'it's just a small script' and skipping it—the autonomous nature of agents means higher costs and potential for compounding errors.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as only for security incidents when it's equally a means to control costs and error compounding.

def: The contract surface between deterministic systems and non-deterministic agents; the only position that leaves traces in records.
pitfall: Wanting something to be auditable but not pushing it to the tool boundary—the model comparing two datasets in its head leaves no trace; calling a diff tool does.
distractor_rationale: Easily understood as API signature when this is really about 'the boundary of observability.'

def: The real feedback the agent gains from the environment at each step during execution, such as tool call results and code execution results.
pitfall: Errors are also ground truth—if you give a cryptic error code, the agent can only guess its way forward.
distractor_rationale: Often confused with 'standard answer' when this refers to facts returned by the environment, not evaluation labels.

def: The complete tool name and parameters for each tool call in a run, plus the complete return value or error for each tool response—first-hand evidence.
pitfall: Using the agent's summary instead of the transcript—the summary quietly erases errors and calls that never happened.
distractor_rationale: Easily treated as 'logs' when logs are actually its structured storage format; the transcript itself is the round-trip original text.

def: What the agent writes about itself: wrap-up summaries, reasoning segments, self-assessments after tool execution—secondary material.
pitfall: What it omits is often more important than what it includes, and missing pieces don't raise their hands.
distractor_rationale: Reads professionally and measured, making it easiest to treat as process evidence; the actual method is to trace each number in the self-report back to the transcript.

def: The reasoning process the model writes before giving an answer, abbreviated CoT.
pitfall: Treating CoT as evidence—it's a clue; to catch behavior not mentioned in CoT you must return to the raw transcript.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as 'the model's real internal process' when it's also generated text that can omit things.

def: A reading checklist for transcripts: called wrong tool, called right tool but wrong parameters, called too few tools, processed tool response incorrectly.
pitfall: Evidence for 'too few calls' is absence and won't jump out on its own—you have to use task requirements as a template and count.
distractor_rationale: Originally a tool design taxonomy, easily treated as a bug classification—its real use is pointing each question to a specific location in the transcript for verification.

def: A content block where the model names which tool to call, containing the tool name and a complete parameter object the model generated.
pitfall: Only looking at it and drawing conclusions—it only shows what the model 'wanted' to do; whether it succeeded requires checking the paired tool_result.
distractor_rationale: Parameters are long and look plausible, making them easy to skim; bugs like adding four extra characters to query terms live here.

def: The block the harness sends back after actually running the tool—on success the complete return value, on failure the error content plus an error flag.
pitfall: Just noting 'it errored' and moving on—the real information is in the immediately following assistant message.
distractor_rationale: Easily treated as 'the tool's logs' when it's simultaneously input fed back into the model's context, determining the next step.

def: An error flag on tool results, used to distinguish 'tool returned content' from 'tool threw an error.'
pitfall: The harness swallowing exceptions and only stuffing an empty string back—the model will continue fabricating based on its previous assumption.
distractor_rationale: Flagging true doesn't mean execution halts—errors are typically wrapped back into context and the loop continues.

def: SEO-optimized, high-ranking sources with poor authority; manual testing found early agents consistently preferred them over academic PDFs and personal blogs.
pitfall: This source selection bias is nearly invisible in evals—the answers aren't necessarily wrong and scores keep looking good.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as a content quality issue when it's actually written in that string of URLs actually picked in the transcript.

def: Conversation messages persisted to disk, like Claude Code's JSONL session records written to disk.
pitfall: Other people's transcript formats are their internal implementation that changes between versions; pipelines relying on them can break on any release.
distractor_rationale: Looks like ready-made structured raw records, but it's also asynchronously written—at the moment a hook fires it may not contain recent messages.

def: Turning each step into JSON records with fields, so evidence can be not only read by humans but also filtered, aggregated, and analyzed for distributions.
pitfall: Don't compress a whole loop iteration into one record—you'll never be able to calculate the split between model time and tool time; don't write only one summary record when the task finishes either.
distractor_rationale: Doesn't conflict with raw transcripts—it's just storing the same batch of evidence in a different format, moving from 'one run' to 'two hundred runs.'

def: Log writing that encodes structure into natural language; reads smoothly but can only be decoded by humans.
pitfall: Relying on regex to extract numbers—when someone changes 'took' to 'elapsed,' the regex silently starts returning zero.
distractor_rationale: Better human reading experience, so often considered 'friendlier,' but the cost is complete inability to aggregate.

def: One file where each line is a complete JSON object, no commas between lines and no outer array wrapper—commonly written JSONL.
pitfall: When the process gets killed the last line might be half-written—parsers need to report bad lines without halting the entire batch.
distractor_rationale: Often mistaken as a 'lazy shortcut format' when its real advantages are append-only writes, stream processing, and each line being self-contained.

def: An identifier for one conversation session, constant across multiple turns, used to answer 'how much did this session cost total, did it switch permission modes.'
pitfall: Using it as the grouping key to judge 'whether there was follow-up after an error'—the next prompt in the same session will mask the previous stall.
distractor_rationale: Different granularity from prompt_id but often mixed up: session is one entire conversation, prompt is one trigger within it.

def: An identifier for one user prompt; all model requests and tool calls it triggers share this value.
pitfall: Building the logger with the wrong lifecycle—creating it inside each turn makes session_id a duplicate of prompt_id.
distractor_rationale: The least conspicuous field when writing logs, but its real value shows only when threading scattered records into a tree.

def: An ID number given to 'one trigger event,' and every event that trigger spawned copies it—no infrastructure needed, just a field.
pitfall: It provides a boundary but not structure—after filtering you still have parallel rows; who is whose child requires parent-child fields.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as the entirety of tracing when it's just the first step in adding relationships.

def: Milliseconds a step took, used to find performance bottlenecks and also to check 'is it stuck.'
pitfall: Where the timer starts and stops determines what this number means—whether it includes the tool's own retries and backoff must be defined and written down.
distractor_rationale: The execution milliseconds in hook payloads exclude permission wait and PreToolUse time—using it to answer 'how long did the user wait' will be systematically low.

def: Parameters sent to the tool, directly provided in PostToolUse payloads as half of the complete call record.
pitfall: By default don't write full text in production logs, only record shape and length; turn on full text only for specific troubleshooting after confirming the log destination is approved to store this data type.
distractor_rationale: Often thought to require manual reconstruction from transcripts when it's actually right there in the payload, and more reliable than asynchronously-written transcripts.

def: The result returned by the tool, part of the complete round-trip record that tool_input and tool_response together form in one trigger.
pitfall: To get 'fuller context,' reading the transcript path given in the payload—that will yield intermittently incomplete data that doesn't error.
distractor_rationale: Only present after successful tool execution—to cover 'parameters generated but didn't execute,' pair PreToolUse with it and diff.

def: The error field on records, only present when it fails; the first field to filter when locating.
pitfall: Missing fields not caught become NaN, contaminating the entire aggregate column without erroring.
distractor_rationale: 'Not in the record' doesn't mean 'didn't happen': retry semantics can make a day's worth of jitter not land on disk at all.

def: A set of numbers: runtime for individual tool calls and whole tasks, total tool call count, total token consumption, tool errors.
pitfall: Average duration almost always lies—99 calls at 80ms plus 1 at 30 seconds averages to a number that looks okay, but reality is 99 fast and one completely stalled.
distractor_rationale: Same set used in evaluation, only difference is what you compare them to: before-vs-after, or today-vs-past-seven-days.

def: Lots of repeated tool calls, often suggesting pagination size or token limit parameters need tuning.
pitfall: These calls are each legal and each succeeds, metrics show no 'error,' but they're all waste.
distractor_rationale: Don't just look at 'highest call count'—high count itself isn't the problem; the same tool with only offset advancing is.

def: Lots of errors for invalid parameters, pointing to tool descriptions needing clearer writing or better examples.
pitfall: When errors cluster on the same parameter the signal is extremely strong, but one isolated case doesn't constitute a pattern; don't change descriptions based on it.
distractor_rationale: Investigation direction is the tool description, not the model; execution timeouts and similar errors don't belong to this category.

def: A proportion metric of error count divided by call count, used instead of absolute numbers to see health.
pitfall: Changing the denominator when the numerator hasn't changed—if the count itself didn't cover retries, dividing by anything still gives you zero.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as a universal fix when actually if semantics don't cover something, no formula can rescue it.

def: The error event emitted only after internal retries completely give up, representing 'this request ultimately failed.'
pitfall: Reading 'three errors today' as 'three network hiccups'—underneath hides however many successful retries; this signal says not a word about them.
distractor_rationale: This design is correct, otherwise the error curve would be flooded by transient hiccups that auto-recovery handled; the cost is you must write down the semantics.

def: A state where the last record for a prompt has an error and no subsequent records follow—versus 'recovered from error.'
pitfall: The condition must be 'last record has error'; writing 'exists error' will mislabel runs that errored then recovered and continued.
distractor_rationale: Choosing the wrong grouping key causes missed detection: the next prompt in the same session will be treated as 'follow-up action' after the previous error.

def: The line that judges 'how much counts as abnormal'; no numbers in first-hand materials—wrong error budget and SLO alike.
pitfall: Writing 'after 3 consecutive errors send email' into the harness—that logic gets deployed with the agent, restarted with the agent, and breaks with the agent.
distractor_rationale: The docs mention alerting should be done, easily read as 'the docs gave recommended values.'

def: Security Information and Event Management system; anomaly detection, baselining, cross-session correlation, and alerting are all responsibilities on its side.
pitfall: Having the observed system make its own judgments—it has no historical data to compare against and it breaks along with the main flow.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as purely a security product when here it bears 'all processing beyond the raw event stream.'

def: After attaching end-user identity attributes, tool decisions, tool results, MCP connections, and permission mode changes form a per-user record.
pitfall: Thinking you need to build a separate collection system—it's the same batch of events used for debugging, just sliced differently.
distractor_rationale: Debugging slices horizontally by prompt, auditing slices vertically by user; the same batch of data read two ways is often treated as two separate things.

def: A record of a piece of work with a beginning and end: has a name, start time, end time, several attributes, and can identify its parent span.
pitfall: Tool spans must separate 'waiting for permission' and 'executing' into two segments—the same 40 seconds split reveals whether to fix config or fix implementation.
distractor_rationale: Easily equated with one log line when the difference is it carries a time range and parent-child relationships.

def: An entire tree of spans connected by parent-child relationships; everything that happened in one complete request from start to finish, read as a tree.
pitfall: It's the most expensive and most detailed; adoption order should place it after metrics and log events.
distractor_rationale: Often treated as 'more detailed logs' when what it really gives you beyond logs is belonging relationships and time nesting.

def: The root span name corresponding to each user prompt in first-party traces.
pitfall: Hook executions are also recorded under it—the observability mechanism itself is an observed object.
distractor_rationale: Name sounds like 'one interaction' but its boundary is one prompt, not an entire conversation.

def: A lower-level agent dispatched through the Agent tool; its model requests and tool spans nest under the parent agent's tool span.
pitfall: Tallying by 'only count model requests issued by the main loop'—one prompt's cost can be under-reported by more than half.
distractor_rationale: Records from concurrent runs interleave with the main loop on the timeline; splitting by time window is nearly impossible.

def: The code in the process responsible for packaging spans and sending them out.
pitfall: When running through the SDK don't set console as the exporter value.
distractor_rationale: The three signals each have their own exporter; metrics working doesn't mean traces work.

def: The relay station or backend service that receives spans; the exporter sends data to it, you see the tree on its dashboard.
pitfall: When it responds slowly, the flush before process exit gets cut off by a short timeout, and tail-end spans still drop.
distractor_rationale: Self-hosted collectors are also OTLP backends; you don't need to select a commercial product before starting.

def: The default behavior where when the endpoint is unreachable or the backend rejects data, the agent runs normally, telemetry is dropped, and no error surfaces in your application.
pitfall: A broken pipeline and everything-working look identical on your end; zero data can't be read as 'no problems.'
distractor_rationale: The design itself is correct—the observability pipeline shouldn't bring down the main flow—but the cost is you must verify the probe first when troubleshooting.

def: The mechanism of accumulating telemetry into batches and sending them out on intervals—by default metrics every 60 seconds, traces and logs every 5 seconds.
pitfall: If the process is killed before the CLI shuts down, whatever's in the batch buffer is lost; short-lived runs need intervals significantly shorter than run duration.
distractor_rationale: When encountering missing tails, easily think 'enlarge the batch'—the direction is exactly backwards; the bigger the batch, the worse the loss when the last batch drops.

def: A resource attribute identifying which service data came from; the CLI defaults to reporting it as claude-code.
pitfall: Multiple agents exporting to the same collector without overriding it results in seeing soup.
distractor_rationale: 'Seeing no data' can also mean data arrived but is mixed under someone else's service name—this suspicion ranks after the pipeline.

def: A counting metric emitted as soon as a session starts; the cheapest probe for verifying export config worked.
pitfall: Being able to query it only means the data path is live; next come suspicions about query expressions and panel config.
distractor_rationale: Its value isn't in the metric itself but in splitting 'does the agent have a problem' and 'is the pipeline working' into two separately answerable questions.

def: A standard-format environment variable carrying trace id and current span id; Bash and PowerShell subprocesses automatically inherit it.
pitfall: Hook subprocesses don't get OTEL_* export config; don't expect to piggyback on the harness's telemetry pipeline by inheriting environment variables in hooks.
distractor_rationale: It solves 'who should I attach to,' not 'where does data go'—these two things are often conflated.

def: A standard-format string containing trace id and current span id; whoever receives it knows where to attach themselves.
pitfall: When rebuilding trees it's hidden in a field different from others; after splitting by dash, the third segment is the parent span id.
distractor_rationale: Looks like an auth header when it actually only carries belonging information, no content.

def: The switch that when turned on makes each step of the agent loop become an inspectable span in the tracing backend.
pitfall: Without the switch you'll see a thin or completely empty trace view, easily misjudged as the pipeline not working.
distractor_rationale: It's different from 'the trace signal itself's enable switch'—both must be confirmed.

def: User-defined shell commands, HTTP endpoints, or LLM prompts that execute automatically at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle.
pitfall: Command hooks execute with your full user permissions; review and test before adding them to config.
distractor_rationale: For observability, its value isn't 'can change behavior' but 'can see without changing behavior.'

def: The matching rule that determines when a hook fires; omitted or set to wildcard means one-hook-records-all.
pitfall: When the log is empty, first check the debug log for match records—if written wrong it won't error, just won't fire.
distractor_rationale: In observability scenarios don't narrow it: you don't know in advance which tool will break.

def: An event that runs after the model creates tool parameters and before processing the tool call.
pitfall: Time it spends isn't counted in the execution milliseconds in the payload; don't add them together as one step's duration.
distractor_rationale: The value of this gap is parameters are finalized but the tool hasn't run—bugs like adding a year to query terms live in these parameters.

def: An event that fires after successful tool execution; the input carries both tool_input and tool_response.
pitfall: The trigger condition is 'successful execution'—to cover cases where parameters were generated but execution didn't succeed, pair it with PreToolUse and diff.
distractor_rationale: One firing is one complete round-trip; often thought to require pairing request and response yourself.

def: A once-per-session event; fires when a new session opens and also when an existing session resumes.
pitfall: Writing a handler that 'initializes a new log when session starts' will overwrite the previous segment the first time it hits resume.
distractor_rationale: From the loop's perspective resume isn't 'starting fresh,' but it still rings this event.

def: An end-of-turn event in the once-per-turn cadence; paired with UserPromptSubmit can calculate one turn's duration.
pitfall: Only hooking it without hooking the exception exit means abnormally ended turns never get an end time, and start records hang forever.
distractor_rationale: Choosing the wrong cadence yields numbers hard to explain: wanting to count 'how many tools did one task use' but hooking the per-turn gate only gets you zero.

def: The JSON context handed to your handler when an event fires and the matcher matches.
pitfall: To get 'fuller context,' switching to read the transcript file path it provides—that file is written asynchronously and may not contain the current turn's recent messages.
distractor_rationale: Command hooks receive it from stdin and respond via exit code, stdout/stderr—no magic involved.

def: A set of environment variables related to telemetry export; Claude Code removes them from every subprocess it spawns, including hooks.
pitfall: To emit telemetry in hooks you must carry your own complete export config, or just have it write structured logs and align with telemetry using prompt id.
distractor_rationale: Failure is silent—data won't export but won't error either, so you'll think it's waiting in the backend.

def: A log file that records which hooks matched, their exit codes, and full stdout and stderr.
pitfall: To see finer-grained lines like matcher counts, you need to set log level to verbose.
distractor_rationale: When hooks don't work, it's the only place that can separate 'didn't fire,' 'didn't match,' and 'script crashed.'

def: This course's arranged debugging approach: narrow by prompt id, find first divergence, replay observation, repeatedly stress the same component, recover from failure point after fixing.
pitfall: Walking all five steps has a cost; low-frequency harmless jitter is cheaper to log and accumulate first, investigate when patterns emerge.
distractor_rationale: It's this course's own arrangement, not official methodology—only each step's foundation has sources.

def: Step one: filter by prompt id to shrink the range from 'agent broke' to 'these ten-plus events under this id.'
pitfall: Without this step, every subsequent question can't start—you can't even circle which lines belong to this run.
distractor_rationale: This step's significance isn't technical, it's psychological—turning an undebuggable proposition into a debuggable one.

def: The step where behavior starts deviating from expectations; the absurdities at the end are mostly downstream noise.
pitfall: Fixing the last step is usually cleaning up after an upstream error; swap the failure method and new ones will grow.
distractor_rationale: The hardest kind of divergence to recognize is 'processed the tool response incorrectly'—that step shows green in logs.

def: Steps after the divergence point that look equally absurd but are just continuing forward on the wrong premise.
pitfall: Only getting the final output, people usually go change the prompt to add 'no fabricating'—that hits contagion, doesn't hit the lesion.
distractor_rationale: Contagion steps are genuinely wrong themselves, so extremely easy to treat as independent bugs and fix one by one.

def: Building simulations using identical prompts and tools, watching step-by-step to immediately force failure modes out.
pitfall: Two constraints can't be loosened: input copied as-is, observation must be step-by-step—run once to completion and only check final output makes this pointless.
distractor_rationale: Same bugs invisible in aggregate metrics (success rate is high) and require line-by-line reading in after-the-fact logs, but when watching step-by-step the human eye spots them in seconds.

def: A stand-in that doesn't send network requests, returning preset response objects from a fixed array in sequence, making the model side reproducible.
pitfall: It locks down the environment side; model behavior is still non-deterministic in real runs—this is noise reduction, not a reproduction guarantee.
distractor_rationale: Often said to 'make agents deterministic' when it actually just changes two moving variables to one.

def: The array the stub client draws from in sequence, each element carrying complete stop_reason, content blocks, and usage.
pitfall: When the queue is exhausted, explicitly throw an error and record one; otherwise the last turn has no corresponding record and turn count won't match model call count.
distractor_rationale: The harness loop doesn't change a single word—what it receives is shape-identical to what a real client returns.

def: An agent that, given a flawed tool, repeatedly tries using it then rewrites the tool description to avoid failures; testing dozens of times finds key nuances and bugs.
pitfall: 'Dozens of times' is the point—running three to five times, bugs like 'sometimes fabricates' might not appear once.
distractor_rationale: Stressing a component's behavior at boundary inputs, not vaguely 'running a few more times.'

def: One id per run, threading scattered records in the same stream back to the same run.
pitfall: Whether it's called this or prompt_id doesn't matter; what matters is this id exists and every record carries it.
distractor_rationale: It only circles the range; rebuilding records into a tree still requires parent-child fields.

def: This record's own id; other records point to it to declare 'I'm under you.'
pitfall: Logs are written in end-time order, so children often appear before parents—don't let file order mislead you when reconstructing.
distractor_rationale: Different granularity from trace_id: one trace_id per run, one span_id per step.

def: A field pointing to the parent record's id; trees are reconstructed from on-disk JSONL using this.
pitfall: If something is missing from the tree, that's not a printing-code problem, it's a recording-code problem—what wasn't recorded won't appear in the tree.
distractor_rationale: Parent-child relationships don't rely on in-memory call stacks but on persisted fields; this point makes them work across processes.

def: A hard gate on loop iteration count; exceeding it throws an error, records an interrupt, and exits non-zero.
pitfall: Loops without stopping conditions mean surrendering control; maximum iteration count is the cheapest gate.
distractor_rationale: It governs 'did it run away,' not 'is the output correct'—the latter is the validator's job.

def: The field in model responses that drives the harness loop to continue or finish.
pitfall: When finishing, it being end_turn doesn't mean the task succeeded—the agent might think it smoothly completed while missing a piece of data.
distractor_rationale: It's a control-flow signal, not a quality signal; easily treated as evidence of 'success.'

def: The line defining how many characters maximum each content snippet in logs keeps; set to 0 and not a single word hits disk.
pitfall: Before adjusting it to record full text, the prerequisite is your observability pipeline is approved to store the data type your agent handles—pass approval before changing code.
distractor_rationale: 'Disk is cheap, record everything can't hurt' only holds on the disk dimension; compliance and searchability both take hits.

def: A field in records describing a value's type and scale: is it string or object, how long, what keys.
pitfall: Only counting call count without even recording shape means you can't answer 'which path did that errored read pass.'
distractor_rationale: The dividing line isn't 'record or not' but 'record structure or record content': shape can locate, full text defaults to not landing on disk.

def: One line outputting total rounds, tool call count, tokens, error count, and total duration—one piece of the observability three-part kit.
pitfall: The round count, call count, and tokens for the failing run might be nearly identical to normal runs; the only thing that changed is error count.
distractor_rationale: It answers 'does this run look normal,' not 'is the output correct'—the latter needs separate verification.

def: A comparison script that reads two run logs, compares side-by-side by record type and tool name, and exits non-zero if errors exist.
pitfall: Newly installed gates must first be run comparing a clean run with itself to confirm it genuinely lets through when 'should pass'—otherwise every exit code is untrustworthy.
distractor_rationale: Gates ask 'does this run still have tool errors,' not 'is the final output correct.'

def: A judgment wired to exit codes; non-zero can be caught by CI, cron, or any 'non-zero means alert' place.
pitfall: A check script that always returns 0 is the same as no check script—must construct a counter-example to verify it can distinguish.
distractor_rationale: It only sends the signal out; anomaly detection and alerting are still the backend's responsibilities.
